title: Most distant galaxy proto-supercluster (unannotated)
caption: The proto-supercluster COSMOS-z3.1-A, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Somewhere in this crowded field lies a newly discovered proto-supercluster of galaxies called COSMOS-z3.1-A. Its members are hard to pick out because they are spread widely across the frame against a busy background.

A proto-supercluster is a loose collection of galaxies expected, eventually, to pull together into a stable cluster of clusters. COSMOS-z3.1-A is seen as it was when the Universe was just 2.1 billion years old. According to NOIRLab, that makes it the earliest and most distant proto-supercluster yet found, and its mass is 5000 times that of the Milky Way.

The structure turned up in data from the One-hundred-deg2 DECam Imaging in Narrowbands survey, known as ODIN. The survey uses the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), which the US Department of Energy built. The camera works on NSF's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, located at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile, a program of NSF NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed through broadband g, r and i filters and narrowband N419, N501 and N673 filters, all optical. The color mapping isn't published.

explore: NOIRLab has also released an annotated version of the image that marks the members of COSMOS-z3.1-A, along with an animated 3D model of the structure. The survey behind the discovery, ODIN, uses narrowband filters on the camera.
